meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'No bastard ever won a war by dying for his country. He won it by making the other poor dumb bastard die for his country'?
meta.ogDescription: Patton probably said something like it, but the exact famous wording is George C. Scott's line in the 1970 film Patton. Gavin's 1958 version reads differently.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Patton, and Quote Investigator ↗ believes he used a version of the line in speeches to troops in 1943 and 1944. No transcript pins down this exact wording, though. The famous phrasing is the one George C. Scott speaks in the 1970 film Patton. The earliest Patton-linked print version, James M. Gavin’s 1958 recollection, is worded differently.

source.excerpt: George Patton’s last words to us before we left Africa came home with meaning: ‘No dumb bastard ever won a war by going out and dying for his country. He won it by making some other dumb bastard die for his country.’
trail: Quote Investigator (2015) ↗ says the earliest published evidence it knows of is Gavin’s 1958 book War and Peace in the Space Age. Its conclusion is that Patton used the line in more than one speech in 1943 and 1944, with variable phrasing.
Gavin’s own versions don’t match each other. The 1958 book has “No dumb bastard,” while his February 1965 Atlantic article has “no son of a bitch,” which suggests he was quoting from memory (QI ↗).
Wikiquote ↗ lists the popular wording in its “Misattributed” section as spoken by George C. Scott in the film Patton, and gives Gavin’s 1958 text as a variant.

Wikipedia’s article on Patton’s speech to the Third Army ↗ places the exact popular wording in a 31 May 1944 address to the 6th Armored Division. Its only cited source is a 2010 anthology, B. L. Gist’s Eloquently Speaking (Xlibris), which is not a primary source.
source.excerptNote: This is Gavin’s wording, written down years after the speech, as reproduced by Quote Investigator ↗ and Wikiquote ↗. The popular version (“No bastard … the other poor dumb bastard”) matches the 1970 film. In 1965 Gavin quoted it again as “no son of a bitch ever won a war by dying for his country.”

Both works came out in 1931 or later, so both are treated as in copyright. Patton’s spoken remarks survive only in other people’s later accounts.

author.name: George S. Patton
author.kicker: The general credited with the line
author.heading: About George S. Patton
author.metaLine: 1885–1945 · U.S. Army general, World War II
author.bio: George Smith Patton Jr. was an American general who led U.S. troops in North Africa and Sicily and later commanded the Third Army in Europe. He was famous for profane, unscripted pep talks to his soldiers in 1943 and 1944, and those talks are where this line is reported. His image today owes a lot to George C. Scott’s Oscar-winning performance in the 1970 film Patton.

misattribution.heading: Where the famous wording really comes from
misattribution.intro: The idea is old, Patton probably voiced it, and the polished wording everyone quotes comes from Hollywood.

items.who: Patton (1970 film): George C. Scott, from the screenplay by Francis Ford Coppola & Edmund H. North
items.why: “I want you to remember that no bastard ever won a war by dying for his country. He won it by making the other poor, dumb bastard die for his country” is the film’s line, and Wikiquote ↗ lists it under “Misattributed” for that reason. The film opens with Scott giving a toned-down version of Patton’s speech ↗.
Gavin recalled “No dumb bastard ever won a war by going out and dying for his country” in 1958 and “no son of a bitch” in 1965. As Quote Investigator ↗ documents, even the witness’s wording shifted.

items.who: T. W. H. Crosland (writing as “X”), War Poems, 1917
items.why: Crosland’s poem “Dying for Your Country” has the lines “Don’t die for your dear country’s sake, / But let the other chap die for his.” QI also traces the sentiment to 1883 and to 1942 press quips, all before Patton’s speeches (QI ↗).
This date and audience come from Wikipedia ↗, which cites a 2010 Xlibris anthology. It does not appear in Quote Investigator’s chronology, and we found no primary transcript behind it.

misattribution.truthLine: Patton very likely said something like this to his troops in 1943–44, but the exact words people quote are the 1970 film’s, not a transcript of Patton (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why the movie version won
lead: Patton gave his pep talks to troops without notes, and their wording changed from one telling to the next, so no single authoritative text exists. The line reached the public through people who heard it and wrote it down years later, first James M. Gavin in 1958 and later other memoirists. QI cites a 2004 book that recalls a 5 June 1944 speech using the phrase “no poor bastard ever won a war by dying for his country.”

The 1970 film Patton fixed one smooth version in popular memory. It opens with George C. Scott in front of a giant American flag, delivering a cleaned-up version of the speech. Scott’s line is the one that gets repeated, and that is why the popular wording follows the screenplay rather than any record of Patton himself.
context.detailsSummary: What the sources do and don’t show
detailsBody: Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that Patton “did employ this line in more than one speech in 1943 and 1944,” and adds that the phrasing varied and that precursors were already in circulation.
According to Wikipedia ↗, the screenwriters had to tone down Patton’s language to avoid an R rating. The film’s opening monologue is a dramatization, not a transcript.
context.pull: The idea was Patton’s to borrow; the polish was Hollywood’s.
